messages:
matthew: customer reporting intermittent 504s and lots of "context canceled" in our proxy logs when using our Go SDK. they say it started after they added a retry wrapper around the client.

matthew: short repro they sent (trimmed):
```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 10*time.Second)
defer cancel()
client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
for i := 0; i < 3; i++ {
    // reusing same ctx across retries
    req, _ := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, "POST", url, bytes.NewReader(body))
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    if err == nil && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
        return resp, nil
    }
    time.Sleep(500 * time.Millisecond)
}
```

matthew: logs show lots of: `context canceled` then a downstream 504 at the proxy level.

julie: thanks matthew. quick thought: reusing the same ctx across retries is a common footgun. if the first attempt blocks for e.g. 8s, the ctx remaining time can be tiny and the second attempt immediately sees deadline exceeded.

brian: also check the http.Client Timeout vs context timeout semantics. client.Timeout wraps the entire request (including body read). With a context deadline and client.Timeout both present, whichever finishes first cancels the request. If you reuse ctx across attempts you get cascading early cancels.

aaron: +1. Another pattern we see: people put per-RPC context.WithTimeout at top and then loop; that means retries share the same deadline window. Instead create a fresh per-attempt ctx derived from the parent, e.g.:
```go
// top-level parentCtx has overall deadline/trace/cancel
for i := 0; i < opts.Retries; i++ {
    attemptCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(parentCtx, perAttemptTimeout)
    req = req.WithContext(attemptCtx)
    resp, err := client.Do(req)
    cancel()
    if err == nil { return resp, nil }
}
```

matthew: good catch. customer was using a single parent ctx with 10s and client.Timeout 30s. they also had a custom retry backoff which retried fast, so second attempt immediately got ctx deadline.

julie: aside: also look at transport settings. if IdleConnTimeout/MaxIdleConnsPerHost are too low you can get connection churn + TCP handshake latency that pushes attempts long. recommend tuning transport for high QPS customers:
```go
tr := &http.Transport{
    MaxIdleConns: 100,
    MaxIdleConnsPerHost: 100,
    IdleConnTimeout: 90 * time.Second,
    DisableKeepAlives: false,
}
client := &http.Client{Transport: tr, Timeout: 0} // consider using per-attempt ctx for timeouts
```

brian: also watch for `http.Transport` and TLS handshake reuse issues if they're using custom DialContext with aggressive timeouts. setting DialContext deadlines too low can cause connection setup failures that look like 504s at higher layers.

aaron: one more gotcha: if retry wrapper consumes the original request body (e.g., io.ReadCloser) without rewinding, subsequent attempts will send an empty body and the server may return 400/504. make sure to buffer or re-create the body between attempts.

matthew: customer logs did show "EOF" and empty body at times. they were using bytes.NewBuffer which is fine, but they passed the same ReadCloser around in their wrapper.

julie: proposed remediation steps for customer:
- ensure per-attempt ctx (do not reuse parent per-RPC ctx across retries)
- move timeout control to per-attempt context instead of client.Timeout (or set client.Timeout conservatively)
- tune Transport (MaxIdleConnsPerHost, IdleConnTimeout)
- ensure body is re-readable or recreate it per attempt
- add some jitter to backoff so retries don't pile up at same deadline window

matthew: sample patch we recommended:
```go
parentCtx, pCancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 60*time.Second)
defer pCancel()
for i := 0; i < 4; i++ {
    attemptCtx, aCancel := context.WithTimeout(parentCtx, 8*time.Second)
    reqCopy := cloneRequestWithBody(originalReq) // small helper to copy body
    reqCopy = reqCopy.WithContext(attemptCtx)
    resp, err := client.Do(reqCopy)
    aCancel()
    if err == nil && resp.StatusCode < 500 { return resp, nil }
    time.Sleep(time.Duration(math.Pow(2, float64(i))) * 150 * time.Millisecond)
}
```

brian: if customer still sees 504s after these changes, ask for tcpdump/trace, and check proxy idle timeouts. sometimes edge proxy is dropping long-lived connections when backend pauses.

ops-bot: created support-ticket #SUP-11234 and linked this thread. assigned to oncall: @brian.

matthew: I'll push the code suggestions to the customer and ask them to test. thanks everyone. :thumbsup:

julie: follow-up: got confirmation from customer that switching to per-attempt ctx fixed the sudden 504 spike in their staging environment. they still want guidance on client.Timeout vs per-attempt timeout best-practice; we suggested using client.Timeout=0 and always controlling deadlines with contexts so it's explicit and testable.

aaron: closing notes: add an FAQ entry in support docs about "Go SDK retries and context gotchas" summarizing the above patterns.

matthew: noted, I'll draft the FAQ and link to sample snippets.
